h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Large batches give few optimizer steps in the fixed epoch budget, so a larger step size compensates for the missing updates.
Deeper ReLU stacks compound update-induced activation drift, so they become unstable at smaller learning rates than shallow nets.
Fewer updates at an already tiny step size starve training in a fixed epoch budget.
The per-batch L2 term scales as alpha/batch, so a larger batch weakens an otherwise over-strong penalty and reduces collapse.
The L2 term is divided by batch size, so small batches feel a much stronger effective penalty and more alpha over-shrinks the weights.
The penalty sums over all weights, so very wide nets carry a much larger total shrinkage and are over-regularized sooner.
At tiny learning rates extra width speeds up function-space progress under Adam, easing the undertraining.
Wider layers amplify the effective change per Adam update, so adding width worsens instability near the failure regime.
Narrow single-layer nets are capacity-bottlenecked, so an extra layer adds representational power that wide nets already have.
Strong L2 shrinks each added layer multiplicatively toward a near-constant output, so extra depth hurts more.
